meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Life has become better, comrades; life has become more cheerful'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Stalin: said at the First All-Union Conference of Stakhanovites, 17 Nov 1935. The popular English is one of several translations of the Russian.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Stalin said it in his Speech at the First All-Union Conference of Stakhanovites ↗ on 17 November 1935. The Russian original, “Жить стало лучше, товарищи. Жить стало веселее,” is confirmed in his Collected Works ↗. The popular English is a close, literal rendering. The standard Works translation reads “Life has improved, comrades. Life has become more joyous.”

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Speech at the First All-Union Conference of Stakhanovites
J. V. Stalin, Works, Vol. 14 (Red Star Press, London, 1978), via the Marxists Internet Archive

source.excerpt: The basis for the Stakhanov movement was first and foremost the radical improvement in the material welfare of the workers. Life has improved, comrades. Life has become more joyous. And when life is joyous, work goes well.
trail: The Russian text in Stalin’s Sochineniya, vol. 14, contains “Жить стало лучше, товарищи. Жить стало веселее” and notes that the speech was first published in Pravda on 22 November 1935 — Marxists Internet Archive (Russian) ↗
The English Works, Vol. 14 (Red Star Press, London, 1978), renders it “Life has improved, comrades. Life has become more joyous.” — Marxists Internet Archive (English) ↗
Wikiquote lists “Life has improved, comrades. Life has become more joyous” among Stalin’s sourced quotes, citing the Speech at the Conference of Stakhanovites (17 November 1935) — Wikiquote ↗
Wikipedia says the familiar “Life has become better, life has become joyous” is a widespread version of this phrase from the 17 November 1935 conference — Wikipedia ↗
source.cutTag: Section 2 — The Roots of the Stakhanov Movement
source.excerptNote: Russian original: “Жить стало лучше, товарищи. Жить стало веселее. А когда весело живется, работа спорится.” Translated word for word, the first two sentences give the popular wording, “Life has become better, comrades; life has become more cheerful.” Other English versions use “more joyous,” “merrier” or “happier.”

sourceLink.text: Read the speech in English (Marxists Internet Archive)

source.rightsNote: The speech was first published in 1935, after the 1931 cutoff. The popular English wording is an anonymous literal rendering with no identifiable translator. The Works translation shown above was published in 1978. The Marxists Internet Archive labels its transcription public domain, but that label does not settle US status, so we assert none.

author.name: Joseph Stalin
author.heading: About Joseph Stalin
author.bio: Joseph Stalin led the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until his death in 1953. In 1935 he championed the Stakhanovite movement, a state campaign that celebrated record-breaking workers. He told its first national conference that those records grew from workers’ better material conditions, and that is where this line comes from.

misattribution.heading: Real quote, shifting words
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound: Stalin really said this. But no single English wording is “the” quote. The Russian has been translated several ways, and it often reaches readers through a later song or a slogan rather than through the speech itself.

items.who: “Life has improved, comrades. Life has become more joyous.”
items.why: This is the wording of the English Works edition, and it is the version Wikiquote lists as sourced — Marxists Internet Archive ↗.

items.who: “Life has become better, and happier too.”
items.why: A looser rendering, used in Michigan State’s Seventeen Moments in Soviet History. It notes that Stalin’s words became the motto of the Stakhanovite movement — Seventeen Moments ↗.

Vasily Lebedev-Kumach (words) and Alexander Alexandrov (music) built a song around the phrase. The song is a later reuse, not the source, so the line should be credited to Stalin’s 1935 speech — Wikipedia ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Stalin’s own words, in his 17 November 1935 speech to the Stakhanovites: “Жить стало лучше, товарищи. Жить стало веселее” — Collected Works, vol. 14 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Stalin used the line to explain where the Stakhanovites’ record outputs came from. He said they rested “first and foremost” on improved material welfare, and that “when life is joyous, work goes well.” The phrase became the motto of the Stakhanovite movement and was soon set to music.
In modern Russian the phrase is used ironically, according to Wikipedia ↗. Today it is often quoted as a byword for official cheer that did not match ordinary experience.
